rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is a God-given standard for distinguishing good from evil; Muslims need its true knowledge and practice, not recitation merely for reward or commercial use.
rows.anchor: barometer between good and evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True Qur’anic knowledge reforms the community through practice, following the way its earliest generations were reformed.
rows.anchor: blessed hands of such people that this ummah can be reformed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He undertook the tafsir as an obligation, despite seeing it as a hazardous undertaking whose completion was not assured.
rows.anchor: I have been compelled to write it to fulfill an obligation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When severe illness stopped his mental work in 1971–72, he accepted that the tafsir might remain unfinished as God willed.
rows.anchor: when I fell severely ill in 1971-72, and my doctors stopped me from doing mental work

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He thought reaching Sūrah Tawbah would suffice to demonstrate the truth and value of his late mentor’s interpretive principles.
rows.anchor: demonstrate the veracity and value of the principles

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After recovery and relocation to a village with few amenities, he resolved to write Tadabbur-i Qur’an as gratitude for renewed strength.
rows.anchor: Writing anything else would amount to showing ingratitude to the Almighty Who had once again blessed me with the power and strength to write

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He composed many sūrah commentaries outdoors under trees amid heat, birds, hornets, and flies, absorbed in explaining difficult verses.
rows.anchor: would face an onslaught from birds and hornets from above

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He regarded writing as his duty, while publication and sales were not his responsibility.
rows.anchor: My task was not to print and sell it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His household lived on land inherited by his wife, and he trusted God to provide for him in old age.
rows.anchor: remained with my wife

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reports that scholars and educated readers across regions value the tafsir’s method, which is being used for Qur’anic teaching and studied in research.
rows.anchor: right methodology in understanding and teaching

rows.speaker: Farāhī
rows.claim: His mentor urged complete research and deliberation before writing or speaking, since strong reasoning endures and weak arguments soon disappear.
rows.anchor: after complete research and a lot of deliberation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tafsir does not claim to encompass Qur’anic knowledge; the Qur’an is inexhaustible, and the work only opens a way to deliberate on it.
rows.anchor: unfathomable sea of knowledge and wisdom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Applying the tafsir’s principles can reveal Qur’anic wisdom, help judge disputes across disciplines, and loosen sectarian blind following; later scholars must continue the work.
rows.anchor: they will be able to access the treasures of wisdom which are found in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers should assess what is said rather than who said it, because truth belongs to everyone and failing to recognize it harms the rejecter.
rows.anchor: they should not see who has expressed a particular opinion; they should only see what has been expressed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On finishing the tafsir, he prayed that God accept his service to the Qur’an and make it a means of salvation, asking readers to say amen.
rows.anchor: please accept my effort, and make it a means of my salvation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He credits Ghulām Ṣamdānī with devoted, skillful copying of the manuscripts, more help than even his sons.
rows.anchor: copy the manuscripts of the book with great devotion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Abdullāh Ghulām Aḥmad helped copy the manuscript and used his intelligence to resolve exegetical problems.
rows.anchor: had a great share in this copying out

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalīd Mas‘ūd and Javed Aḥmad helped locate references for citations.
rows.anchor: helped me in locating certain other references

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Majid Khāwar took charge of publication under a schedule and successfully completed it as promised.
rows.anchor: he came forward and assured me that he himself will take up this task according to a program

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He thanks his collaborators and prays that God grant them service that brings success in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: I am grateful to all these friends

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Muzzammil and Sūrah al-Muddaththir form a pair with a shared mood and theme.
rows.anchor: together they form a pair

rows.speaker: Most exegetes
rows.claim: Most exegetes date both sūrahs very early in the Makkan period; Islahi instead reads the contents as a time of intensified Quraysh opposition.
rows.anchor: regard them to be very early

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contents place the address when affluent Quraysh opposition had become intense and the Prophet was distressed by attacks from those he was sent to reform.
rows.anchor: a deliberation on their contents reveals

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shawl depicts the Prophet’s instinct to withdraw into solitude, where he could turn inward and find comfort in nearness to God.
rows.anchor: it is only his shawl which affords him the opportunity to immerse himself deep into his soul

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets are deeply caring and responsible; when opposition grows despite their efforts, they examine themselves and withdraw to seek a solution.
rows.anchor: they thought that perhaps they themselves were at fault

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–14 prescribe night prayer with measured Qur’anic recitation to strengthen the Prophet for his mission, alongside daytime remembrance, trust in God, patience, and leaving enemies to divine judgment.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is directed to regularly offer the tahajjud prayer by night

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 15–19 warn Quraysh by comparing their messenger with Moses before Pharaoh and recalling Pharaoh’s fate and the terrifying Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: just as the Almighty had sent the Prophet Moses (sws) to the Pharaoh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 20, revealed in Madinah, reduces the earlier night-prayer requirement and offers alternatives that preserve its purpose in changed circumstances.
rows.anchor: being reduced in their extent

none: Qur’anic text and its English translation only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muzzammil derives from mutazammil through assimilation of tā into zā, as with muddaththir; the address reflects the Prophet’s inner state.
rows.anchor: the letter ت has been assimilated into ز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet wrapped himself in worry because people rejected his warning and treated his concern as madness.
rows.anchor: would pounce on the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shawl was ordinary Arabic dress; reports also describe the Prophet’s pre-prophethood search for truth and seclusion until God showed him the light, as Sūrah al-Ḍuḥā recalls.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) would search earnestly the truth

rows.speaker: Some of our exegetes
rows.claim: Some exegetes say the address found the Prophet asleep in his shawl; Islahi rejects this because he was never carefree or indifferent to God, and the Qur’an instead depicts his anxiety and prescribes prayer to strengthen him.
rows.anchor: Some of our exegetes are of the opinion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an often lovingly reproaches the Prophet for taking on more than required, while advising prayer when preaching hardship caused him anxiety.
rows.anchor: for burdening himself with much more than what was required

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night prayer is the remedy for the anxiety in the address and brings blessings that renew energy and strengthen faith and resolve.
rows.anchor: this prayer rejuvenates his energy and strengthens his faith and resolve

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer begins after sleep in the latter half of the night; half the night is especially blessed, with latitude for a little less or more because waking is difficult.
rows.anchor: night refers to the last half of the night when a person gets up after sleeping awhile

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an should be recited in a slow, measured manner during the prayer.
rows.anchor: it should be read in slow measured tones

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet recited melodiously, paused at verses, sometimes repeated them emotionally, sought refuge at warnings, thanked God at mercy, and prostrated when prompted; reflective recitation follows Qur’anic guidance, unlike reward-only recitation.
rows.anchor: with a melodious and tuneful voice

rows.speaker: Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī identifies the heavy word as the duty of public warning in Sūrah al-Muddaththir, a view Islahi endorses; later came acquittal, migration, and war.
rows.anchor: Far āhī regards it to mean the responsibility

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night prayer prepares the Prophet and his companions for the struggle to establish Islam by building knowledge of God, faith, resolve, and trust before material means are available.
rows.anchor: struggle for the establishment of Islam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāshi’at al-layl is a verbal noun from ‘to get up’ and means standing at night after rising from sleep, in its later portion.
rows.anchor: It is evident from this word that the time of tahajjud

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rising for night prayer gives a person strength to overcome base desires and reform the soul.
rows.anchor: power and strength to overcome his base desires

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God reserves the latter night for blessings, and its doors are opened to those who value this time and seek His mercy.
rows.anchor: those who value it and come to the presence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Firmly grounded feet portrays a devoted mind, peaceful heart, and alert intellect, reading outward posture as the inner state.
rows.anchor: complete devotion of the mind, peace of the heart

rows.speaker: Some exegetes
rows.claim: Some exegetes understand the phrase as night prayer trampling the soul; Islahi says this is linguistically possible but conflicts with the later verses.
rows.anchor: Some exegetes have taken it to mean that getting up in the night is a means of fully trampling one’s soul

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic speech at night reaches the heart and intellect; the jinn who heard the Prophet reciting in tahajjud embraced faith and called others, as did ‘Umar after hearing the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: so deeply moved by it that they not only embraced faith

rows.speaker: Some exegetes
rows.claim: A common interpretation is that the Prophet’s daytime responsibilities leave little time for concentrated prayer, making tahajjud especially necessary.
rows.anchor: Generally people are of the opinion that this verse tells the Prophet (sws) that he has a lot of other work to do during the day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects the common reading that daytime busyness explains the verse: the night is inherently suited to prayer; sabḥ rarely means being busy without contextual evidence, and tawīlan fits the sense of glorification better than busyness.
rows.anchor: For these reasons, I am unable to convince myself of the conventional interpretation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse calls for daytime glorification as well as night prayer; the Prophet remembered God in daily activities, and transmitted supplications can turn ordinary routines into worship.
rows.anchor: the meaning of the verse is that besides the tahajjud prayer which the Prophet must offer at night, during the day also he has a lot of time for glorifying the Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Continual remembrance is essential to spiritual life: forgetting God leaves the soul lifeless, while remembrance keeps the heart alive.
rows.anchor: his soul becomes lifeless. It is

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling people to religion and reflecting on God’s inward and outward signs are remembrance; reflection makes it meaningful, while remembrance without reflection is only tongue exercise.
rows.anchor: remembrance becomes merely an exercise of the tongue
